blocks.text: A 70-year-old woman with right lower lobe pneumonia has an arterial oxygen saturation of 86 per cent on room air. Giving her oxygen through a mask helps a little, but not as much as her doctors expected. Understanding why requires three ideas: how gases cross the alveolar wall, how well ventilation and blood flow are matched, and how haemoglobin carries oxygen.

blocks.markdown: Gas exchange happens by **passive diffusion** across the **alveolar-capillary membrane**, a barrier less than a micrometre thick formed by alveolar epithelium, a shared basement membrane and capillary endothelium. Each gas moves down its own partial pressure gradient, from high to low. Fick's law tells us what determines the rate.

blocks.caption: Fick's law of diffusion: A is membrane area, D the diffusion coefficient of the gas (which rises with solubility and falls with molecular size), P1 - P2 the partial pressure difference, T the membrane thickness.

rows: Set by the balance of ventilation, oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide output
Mixed venous blood entering pulmonary capillary
Slightly below alveolar PO2 because of a small physiological shunt and V/Q inequality
blocks.caption: Typical partial pressures in healthy young adults at sea level breathing room air. Values are approximate and vary with age and altitude.

blocks.title: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse differently
blocks.text: The pressure gradient for oxygen across the membrane is large (about 60 mmHg) and for carbon dioxide small (about 6 mmHg), yet carbon dioxide equilibrates easily because it is about 20 times more soluble in the membrane and plasma, giving it a much larger diffusion coefficient. In health, blood is fully equilibrated with alveolar PO2 within roughly the first third of its transit time through the capillary, so oxygen uptake is limited by blood flow (perfusion), not diffusion. Diffusion limitation appears only when the membrane is thickened (for example pulmonary fibrosis) or area is lost, particularly during exercise when transit time shortens.

blocks.markdown: Good gas exchange needs ventilated alveoli to be matched to perfused capillaries. The **ventilation-perfusion ratio** compares alveolar ventilation (V, L/min) with blood flow (Q, L/min) for a lung unit or for the whole lung. For the whole lung at rest alveolar ventilation is about 4 L/min and cardiac output about 5 L/min, giving a ratio of about 0.8. Because gravity affects blood flow more than ventilation, the ratio is highest at the apex and lowest at the base of an upright lung.

blocks.title: V/Q ratio and gas composition in a damaged lung unit
blocks.prompt: A lobe receives 1.2 L/min of blood flow, but because of mucus plugging its alveolar ventilation is only 0.6 L/min. Calculate its V/Q ratio and predict its alveolar and end-capillary blood gases relative to a normal unit.

steps.text: A ratio of 0.5 is below the normal 0.8, so blood flow is excessive for the oxygen being delivered. Oxygen is removed from the alveoli faster than ventilation replenishes it, so alveolar PO2 falls, and carbon dioxide arrives faster than it is washed out, so alveolar PCO2 rises.
Blood equilibrates with this alveolar gas, so end-capillary blood leaves with lower PO2 and lower haemoglobin saturation, and mixes with blood from better units, lowering arterial PO2.

blocks.answer: V/Q = 0.5. This low-V/Q unit has low alveolar PO2 and high PCO2, and contributes desaturated blood, causing hypoxaemia.

rows: Alveoli filled with pus or fluid; collapse
Mixed venous gas (PO2 about 40, PCO2 about 46)
Venous blood passes unchanged: severe hypoxaemia, poorly corrected by supplemental oxygen
Lower PO2 and higher PCO2 than normal
No gas exchange from that unit; wasted ventilation
blocks.caption: The V/Q spectrum, from perfusion without ventilation to ventilation without perfusion.

blocks.title: Why overventilated units cannot rescue underventilated ones
blocks.text: Blood leaving a well-ventilated alveolus is already about 97 to 98 per cent saturated, on the flat upper part of the oxygen-haemoglobin curve, so extra ventilation adds almost no oxygen (only a tiny dissolved amount). Hence good units cannot make up for the desaturated blood from poor units, and mixed arterial PO2 falls. Carbon dioxide, which is carried with a nearly linear relationship, can be compensated by increased ventilation of the good units, which is why V/Q mismatch typically lowers oxygen far more than it raises carbon dioxide.

blocks.markdown: In blood, oxygen is carried almost entirely bound to **haemoglobin** (Hb): each gram can bind about 1.34 mL of oxygen. A small amount is dissolved in plasma, 0.003 mL per dL for each mmHg of PO2. The total **oxygen content** therefore depends on haemoglobin concentration and saturation as well as on PO2, and a patient with anaemia can have a normal PO2 yet a low content. The oxygen released to the tissues from each dL of blood is the fall in content between arterial and venous blood; ignoring the small dissolved part, it equals 1.34 x [Hb] x (arterial saturation minus venous saturation), and the dissociation curve (below) tells us how much saturation falls for a given fall in PO2.

blocks.caption: Oxygen content: [Hb] in g/dL, SO2 as a fraction (0 to 1), PO2 in mmHg.

blocks.title: Oxygen content in a healthy adult
blocks.prompt: A healthy adult has haemoglobin 15 g/dL, arterial saturation 0.98 and arterial PO2 100 mmHg. Calculate the arterial oxygen content.

steps.text: Add the two: 19.7 + 0.3 = 20.0 mL/dL. Note that 98 per cent of the oxygen is bound to haemoglobin.

blocks.answer: Arterial oxygen content is about 20 mL/dL, almost entirely bound to haemoglobin.

blocks.markdown: The **oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve** plots saturation against PO2. It is S-shaped because binding of the first oxygen molecules makes later ones easier (cooperativity). The upper flat portion, above a PO2 of about 60 mmHg (saturation about 90 per cent), means saturation stays high even if alveolar PO2 falls modestly; the steep portion between roughly 20 and 40 mmHg means tissues can unload a large amount of oxygen for a small fall in PO2. The **P50**, the PO2 at which Hb is 50 per cent saturated, is about 27 mmHg and measures affinity.

rows: Raised PCO2, raised H+ (lower pH, the Bohr effect), raised temperature, raised 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate
Easier oxygen unloading in active tissues
Lower PCO2, lower H+ (higher pH), lower temperature, lower 2,3-BPG, fetal haemoglobin, carbon monoxide
Oxygen held more tightly, harder to unload
blocks.caption: Factors shifting the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with more than 200 times the affinity of oxygen, lowering oxygen content and also shifting the curve left.

points: Gases cross the alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion down partial pressure gradients; Fick's law makes rate proportional to area, diffusion coefficient and pressure difference, and inversely proportional to thickness.
Carbon dioxide diffuses about 20 times more readily than oxygen; oxygen uptake is normally perfusion-limited and becomes diffusion-limited only in membrane disease or strenuous exercise.

V/Q mismatch (low V/Q units and shunt) is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia; shunt responds poorly to supplemental oxygen, and good units cannot compensate for poor ones because of the flat top of the dissociation curve.

Oxygen content = 1.34 x Hb x saturation + 0.003 x PO2; oxygen unloaded = 1.34 x Hb x (arterial minus venous saturation); a right shift (higher CO2, H+, temperature or 2,3-BPG) raises P50 and aids unloading, a left shift does the opposite.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient with pulmonary fibrosis has a markedly thickened alveolar-capillary membrane. According to Fick's law, which change in the determinants of diffusion best explains reduced gas transfer?

options.text: Increased membrane thickness, which reduces the diffusion rate
Decreased partial pressure of the gas in the blood, which increases the gradient
Increased membrane surface area, which reduces the diffusion rate
Increased solubility of the gas, which reduces its diffusion coefficient

questions.correctOptionText: Increased membrane thickness, which reduces the diffusion rate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rate is inversely proportional to thickness, so a thicker membrane slows diffusion.
distractorRationale.b: A lower blood partial pressure would increase the gradient and rate, not reduce it, and is not the fibrosis mechanism.
distractorRationale.c: Greater area would increase diffusion, and fibrosis does not increase area.
distractorRationale.d: Greater solubility increases the diffusion coefficient and speeds diffusion.

questions.explanation: Fick's law makes diffusion rate proportional to area, diffusion coefficient and pressure difference, and inversely proportional to thickness. Fibrosis thickens the barrier (and can reduce area), slowing diffusion, an effect that is most evident in exercise when blood transit time is short.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide has a much smaller alveolar-capillary partial pressure gradient (about 6 mmHg) than oxygen (about 60 mmHg), yet it equilibrates across the membrane readily. What is the main explanation?

options.text: The membrane is thinner for carbon dioxide than for oxygen
Carbon dioxide is much more soluble, giving a diffusion coefficient about 20 times that of oxygen
Carbon dioxide is actively transported across the membrane
Haemoglobin binds carbon dioxide with greater affinity than oxygen, increasing the gradient

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon dioxide is much more soluble, giving a diffusion coefficient about 20 times that of oxygen

distractorRationale.a: Both gases cross the same membrane, so thickness is identical.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: solubility raises the diffusion coefficient, compensating for the small gradient.
distractorRationale.c: Both gases cross by passive diffusion; no active transport is involved.
distractorRationale.d: Haemoglobin does not account for the diffusion across the membrane, and carbon dioxide is carried largely in other forms.

questions.explanation: Diffusion rate depends on the diffusion coefficient as well as the pressure gradient, and the coefficient rises with solubility. Carbon dioxide is about 20 times more soluble than oxygen, so even a small partial pressure gradient produces rapid transfer.

questions.stem: A cyclist with haemoglobin 15 g/dL has an arterial oxygen saturation of 0.98. Blood leaving his working muscle, where PCO2, H+ and temperature are raised and the dissociation curve is shifted right, has a saturation of 0.40. Ignoring dissolved oxygen and using 1.34 mL O2 per g Hb, calculate the oxygen released to the tissues from each dL of blood, in mL O2 per dL.
questions.explanation: The oxygen released is the fall in haemoglobin-bound oxygen, 1.34 x 15 x (0.98 - 0.40) = 1.34 x 15 x 0.58 = 11.66 mL/dL. At rest, with venous saturation near 0.75, only about 4 mL/dL is released, so the large fall in saturation at the low PO2 of active muscle, helped by the right shift of the curve, is what lets exercising tissue extract much more oxygen.

questions.stem: A lung unit has an alveolar ventilation of 0.9 L/min and a blood flow of 1.5 L/min. Calculate its ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) ratio. The answer is a dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: The V/Q ratio is alveolar ventilation divided by perfusion, 0.9 / 1.5 = 0.6. This is below the normal whole-lung value of about 0.8, so the unit is relatively underventilated and tends towards low alveolar PO2 and high PCO2.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man develops complete collapse (atelectasis) of his left lower lobe after surgery, but the lobe is still perfused. His arterial PO2 rises only slightly when he breathes 100 per cent oxygen. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Oxygen cannot diffuse across a normal alveolar-capillary membrane
Blood passing the collapsed lobe is not exposed to any alveolar gas, so it remains venous (shunt) and mixes with oxygenated blood
The collapsed lobe is ventilated but not perfused, producing dead space
Carbon dioxide displaces oxygen from haemoglobin in the healthy lung

questions.correctOptionText: Blood passing the collapsed lobe is not exposed to any alveolar gas, so it remains venous (shunt) and mixes with oxygenated blood

distractorRationale.a: Oxygen diffuses readily across a normal membrane; the problem is that the affected lobe is not ventilated.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: perfused but unventilated alveoli are a shunt, and extra oxygen cannot reach this blood.
distractorRationale.c: Dead space is ventilated without perfusion, which is the opposite of what is described.
distractorRationale.d: Carbon dioxide does not explain the failure of oxygen to improve saturation in this vignette.

questions.explanation: A collapsed but perfused lobe has a V/Q ratio near zero, a shunt, so blood passes through it without meeting any oxygen-rich gas. Supplemental oxygen raises PO2 only in ventilated units, which are already nearly saturated, so arterial oxygenation improves little.

questions.stem: In a patient with a large low-V/Q region of lung, why does increased ventilation of the healthy regions fail to restore a normal arterial oxygen content?

options.text: Blood from healthy regions is already nearly fully saturated on the flat part of the dissociation curve, so higher PO2 adds little oxygen
Extra ventilation lowers the PO2 of healthy regions
Haemoglobin loses its capacity to bind oxygen when ventilation increases
Oxygen is not soluble in plasma, so it cannot be carried at all

questions.correctOptionText: Blood from healthy regions is already nearly fully saturated on the flat part of the dissociation curve, so higher PO2 adds little oxygen

distractorRationale.a: Correct: saturation is about 97 to 98 per cent already, so further PO2 rises add almost nothing.
distractorRationale.b: More ventilation of healthy units raises, not lowers, alveolar PO2.
distractorRationale.c: Haemoglobin's capacity is not changed by ventilation.
distractorRationale.d: Oxygen is slightly soluble, but the amount dissolved is small; this does not explain the failure to compensate.

questions.explanation: The upper portion of the oxygen-haemoglobin curve is flat, so raising PO2 above about 100 mmHg adds only a small amount of dissolved oxygen. Blood from good units therefore cannot offset the desaturated blood from low V/Q units when the two mix.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, which combination of changes in the working muscle shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?

options.text: Fall in temperature, fall in PCO2 and rise in pH
Rise in temperature, rise in PCO2 and rise in hydrogen ion concentration
Rise in temperature, fall in PCO2 and rise in pH
Fall in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and fall in temperature

questions.correctOptionText: Rise in temperature, rise in PCO2 and rise in hydrogen ion concentration

distractorRationale.a: These changes shift the curve to the left.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: raised temperature, PCO2 and H+ all reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
distractorRationale.c: Temperature rise shifts right, but a fall in PCO2 and a rise in pH shift left, so the net direction is mixed.
distractorRationale.d: A fall in 2,3-BPG and in temperature both shift the curve left.

questions.explanation: Raised PCO2 and hydrogen ion concentration (the Bohr effect), higher temperature and more 2,3-BPG all lower the affinity of haemoglobin, raising P50 and shifting the curve right. This promotes oxygen release exactly where metabolic demand is greatest.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic lung disease and ventilation-perfusion mismatch has haemoglobin 14 g/dL, arterial oxygen saturation 0.82 and arterial PO2 50 mmHg. Using 1.34 mL O2 per g Hb and 0.003 mL O2 per dL per mmHg dissolved, calculate his arterial oxygen content in mL O2 per dL.
questions.explanation: Bound oxygen is 1.34 x 14 x 0.82 = 15.38 mL/dL and dissolved oxygen is 0.003 x 50 = 0.15 mL/dL, so the content is about 15.5 mL/dL. Compared with a normal value near 20 mL/dL, this reflects hypoxaemia from the V/Q mismatch (low saturation and PO2) in the face of normal haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Using Fick's law, explain why oxygen transfer is normally perfusion-limited in a healthy resting lung, and describe two circumstances in which it can become diffusion-limited.
markingGuide: States Fick's law: rate proportional to area, diffusion coefficient and partial pressure difference, inversely proportional to thickness
States that in health the thin membrane and large area allow blood to equilibrate with alveolar PO2 within about the first third of the capillary transit time
Concludes that more oxygen is taken up only if more blood flows (perfusion-limited)
Gives a first circumstance: a thickened or scarred membrane, for example pulmonary fibrosis
Gives a second circumstance: reduced surface area, or strenuous exercise with shortened capillary transit time
Explains that in these cases equilibration is not complete before the blood leaves the capillary
questions.explanation: In a healthy lung the membrane is thin, the area is large and the gradient is steep, so blood reaches alveolar PO2 well before the end of the capillary and extra flow, not better diffusion, brings more oxygen. When thickness rises, area falls or transit time shortens, equilibration is incomplete and diffusion becomes the limit.

questions.stem: Explain the physiological significance of a rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve in exercising muscle. In your answer define P50, name three factors that cause the shift, and state the effect on oxygen unloading and on loading in the lungs.
markingGuide: Defines P50 as the PO2 at which haemoglobin is 50 per cent saturated, about 27 mmHg, a measure of affinity
A right shift increases P50 and reduces affinity
Names three of: raised PCO2, raised H+ (Bohr effect), raised temperature, raised 2,3-BPG
Explains that these factors are present in active muscle where metabolism is high
States that oxygen is unloaded more readily at a given tissue PO2
States that loading in the lungs is little affected because the upper part of the curve is flat, so saturation remains high at alveolar PO2
questions.explanation: Exercising muscle produces carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and heat, all of which raise P50 and shift the curve right, so more oxygen is released at a given PO2 exactly where it is needed. Because the upper part of the curve is flat, the reduced affinity barely impairs oxygen loading at the high PO2 of the lungs.
